title: The Von Neumann Model (Von-Neumann-Konzept) and Program Execution
summary: This unit explains the Von Neumann model, its four functional units (Vier Werke), the shared main memory for programs and data (Hauptspeicher), and sequential instruction execution (sequenzielle Befehlsausführung). It also introduces the Harvard architecture (Harvard-Architektur), linking (Linken), self-modifying code (Selbstmodifizierender Code), and the roles of the prologue and epilogue (Prolog und Epilog).
concepts: Shared program and data memory (Programme und Daten im selben Speicher)
keyFacts: The stack resides in byte-addressed main memory.
The prologue sets up the stack frame, and the epilogue tears it down.
The calling convention specifies which registers must be preserved.
With -O2, register allocation or instruction order may differ from unoptimized examples.
The Von Neumann model separates the computer’s structure from the specific problem; the program controls the general-purpose computer.
The four functional units are main memory, the control unit, the arithmetic unit or ALU, and the input/output unit.
In the Von Neumann model, programs and data reside in the same main memory.
Main memory consists of equal-sized cells with consecutive addresses.
Programs and data are represented as encoded memory contents, or binary codes.
In general, instructions are stored and executed sequentially at increasing addresses.
Conditional and unconditional jumps can change the sequential order.
Von Neumann uses shared program and data memory; Harvard uses separate memories.
A shared main memory with separate instruction and data caches is one cited hybrid form.
Write protection and the separation of program and data memory are different questions.
Linking combines compiled program components and libraries, resolves references, and may adjust address information.
Self-modifying code changes its own program code and is now a rare exception.

questions.prompt: Where is the stack located in the computer model under consideration?

options.text: In main memory
Exclusively in the registers
In stack memory separate from main memory
In the input/output unit

questions.explanation: The stack is an area of byte-addressed main memory. It is not a separate memory distinct from main memory.

questions.prompt: At the end of a routine comes the ___, which restores saved values and releases the stack frame.

options.text: Epilogue
Instruction cycle
Linker
Prologue

questions.explanation: The epilogue tears down the frame set up by the prologue and prepares for the return.

questions.prompt: Which mappings to the four functional units are correct? Select all correct statements; more than one answer may be correct.

options.text: The arithmetic unit handles input and output, including secondary storage.
The control unit carries out the instruction cycle.
The input/output unit translates source code into machine instructions.
The arithmetic unit, or ALU, performs arithmetic operations.
Main memory contains programs and data.

questions.explanation: Main memory, the control unit, and the arithmetic unit correspond to mappings a, b, and c. Translation is not the task of the input/output unit, while input and output belong to that unit.

questions.prompt:
Which step in the diagram immediately follows the routine body?

```mermaid
flowchart LR
P["Prolog"] --> R["Routinenkörper"]
R --> E["Epilog"]
E --> C["Rücksprung"]
```

options.text: Stack pointer
Return
Prologue
Epilogue

questions.explanation: The epilogue follows the routine body. It restores saved values and releases the stack frame.

questions.prompt: Which fundamental idea is part of the Von Neumann model?

options.text: A computer consists exclusively of an ALU.
The computer’s structure is independent of the problem; the program controls the general-purpose computer.
The computer’s structure is rebuilt for every problem.
Programs must never reside in main memory.

questions.explanation: The Von Neumann model describes a general-purpose computer whose specific behavior is determined by the program being run.

questions.prompt: In the Von Neumann model, programs and data reside in the same main memory.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Shared main memory for programs and data is a central feature of the Von Neumann model.

questions.prompt: In general, instructions are stored one after another at ___ addresses.

options.text: only external
increasing
decreasing
random

questions.explanation: In general, instructions are stored at increasing addresses. Jumps can later change the execution order.

questions.prompt: Which statements about data and instructions as memory contents are correct? Select all correct statements; more than one answer may be correct.

options.text: Instructions are encoded according to the ISA and can be represented as assembly.
Data are encoded in binary and require an agreed-upon interpretation of their bit patterns.
Only instructions, but not data, exist as memory contents.
The readable assembly representation is identical to the physical memory contents.
Data are always stored in memory as decimal digits.

questions.explanation: Both data and instructions are encoded memory contents. They are interpreted differently: data use an agreed-upon encoding, while instructions follow the ISA.

questions.prompt: What memory organization does the Harvard architecture describe?

options.text: Only instruction memory, with no data memory
A shared main memory with no registers
Separate program and data memories
A shared memory for programs and data

questions.explanation: Harvard separates program memory from data memory. Shared memory, by contrast, is characteristic of Von Neumann.

questions.prompt: What is a central task of the linker?

options.text: It changes only the program’s input data.
It combines compiled program components and libraries and resolves references.
It executes the program step by step.
It replaces the ISA with a different ISA.

questions.explanation: The linker combines compiled components and library components. In doing so, it resolves references and may adjust address information.

questions.prompt: Self-modifying code changes its own program instructions in memory. Today it is considered a rare exception; different execution paths are usually implemented with conditional jumps and changes to addresses. Statement: Self-modifying code is a common standard technique today.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: The statement is false: self-modifying code is considered a rare exception today. Different execution paths are usually implemented with conditional jumps and changes to addresses.

questions.prompt: In the Von Neumann model, which task belongs to the control unit?

options.text: Carry out the instruction cycle
Perform arithmetic operations
Provide input and output, including secondary storage
Store programs and data permanently

questions.explanation: The control unit carries out the instruction cycle. Arithmetic operations belong to the arithmetic unit, and storage belongs to main memory.

questions.prompt: A program starts at address $100$. The instruction at $101$ is an unconditional jump to $200$. Which sequence gives the first addresses executed?
questions.explanation: First $100$ is executed, followed by the jump instruction at $101$. Because the jump unconditionally goes to $200$, the next address is $200$; $102$ is skipped.

The arithmetic unit controls the control unit.
The input/output unit communicates exclusively with the arithmetic unit.

questions.explanation: The directed edge from the control unit to the arithmetic unit is labeled “controls.” The diagram also shows instructions and data in main memory.

questions.prompt: A computer has shared main memory for programs and data, but separate instruction and data caches. What is this organization called?

options.text: Pure Von Neumann architecture with no separate memory areas
Self-modifying memory
Strict Harvard architecture
The hybrid form described

questions.explanation: The hybrid form described combines shared main memory with separate instruction and data caches.

questions.prompt: Which activities are part of linking? Select all correct statements; more than one answer may be correct.

options.text: Execute every instruction during linking
Resolve references between the components being combined
Redefine the target processor’s ISA
Adjust address information if necessary
Combine compiled program components and the required library components

questions.explanation: Linking combines components, resolves their references, and may adjust address information. Executing the program and defining the ISA are not part of it.

questions.prompt: During linking, references between the combined program components are ___, and address information may be adjusted.

options.text: resolved
ignored
encrypted
doubled

questions.explanation: The linker matches references to their targets, thereby resolving them. Address information is adjusted if needed.

questions.prompt: Write protection and the separation of program and data memory are different questions.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: For example, a memory area can be non-modifiable without that automatically determining whether program and data memories are separate.

questions.prompt: What does self-modifying code refer to?

options.text: A compiler optimization level of 2
A program that only reads its input data
A linker that combines libraries
A program that changes its own program code

questions.explanation: Self-modifying programs change their own program code. This is distinct from changing data or from linking.

questions.prompt: A program contains instructions at addresses $40$, $41$, and $42$. The instruction at $41$ is a conditional jump to $100$; the condition is satisfied. Which address is executed next?
questions.explanation: The jump instruction at $41$ sets execution to continue at the target address $100$. Therefore, the normally next address $42$ does not follow.

questions.prompt: What must be preserved when a compiler optimization changes the internal implementation?

options.text: The use of -O2
Exactly the same register allocation
Exactly the same instruction sequence
The externally observable behavior required of the program

questions.explanation: Optimizations may change register allocation and instruction order. What matters is that the program’s externally observable behavior is preserved.

questions.prompt: Which statements correctly describe program execution? Select all correct statements; more than one answer may be correct.

options.text: The basic instruction sequence is initially carried out sequentially.
Every jump must completely prohibit sequential order.
An optimization may work differently internally as long as the observable behavior is preserved.
Optimization necessarily means using the same register allocation as in the example.
Conditional and unconditional jumps can change the order.

questions.explanation: Sequential execution is the starting point, jumps can depart from it, and optimizations may change the internal implementation. Register allocation does not have to remain the same.

source.heading: Wie wird ein Programm schrittweise abgearbeitet?

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes memory organization from memory handling?

options.text: Separate memory areas cannot be write-protected in principle.
A shared memory can never have different access permissions.
Whether program and data memory are shared or separate is a different question from write protection.
Write protection automatically determines whether the architecture is Harvard or Von Neumann.

questions.explanation: Whether memory is shared or separate concerns its organization. Write protection, by contrast, describes how memory areas are handled.

questions.prompt: Which statements about Von Neumann, Harvard, and the hybrid form described are correct? Select all correct statements; more than one answer may be correct.

options.text: Harvard uses separate program and data memories.
Write protection alone turns every shared memory into a Harvard architecture.
With separate caches, programs and data can no longer reside in shared main memory.
Von Neumann uses shared memory for programs and data.
A shared main memory with separate instruction and data caches is one cited hybrid form.

questions.explanation: a, b, and c correspond to the three organizational forms described. Write protection and separate caches do not by themselves fully determine the memory organization.

questions.prompt: Because programs reside in main memory in the Von Neumann model, the machine can in principle also change program contents.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Programs and data reside in the same memory, and the key points explicitly state that the machine can change memory contents.

questions.prompt: Which technique is cited as the usual way to implement different execution paths without changing the program’s own code?

options.text: Deleting main memory exclusively
Conditional jumps and changes to addresses
Replacing the ALU with the input/output unit
Storing all instructions as decimal numbers

questions.explanation: Instead of self-modifying code, different execution paths are implemented mainly through conditional jumps and address changes.

questions.prompt: During linking, references are resolved and, if necessary, ___ are adjusted.

options.text: address information
input/output units
instruction cycles
register widths

questions.explanation: The linker can adjust address information so that references between the combined program components point to the correct targets.

questions.prompt: Which statements about optimization and program execution are correct? Select all correct statements; more than one answer may be correct.

options.text: The externally observable behavior must be preserved.
Optimization may change the required behavior arbitrarily.
After every optimization, the sequential principle applies completely, with no possible jumps.
An optimized program does not have to use the same instruction sequence as an unoptimized example.
An optimized program does not have to use the same register allocation as an unoptimized example.

questions.explanation: Optimizations can change register allocation and instruction order. The program’s observable behavior must still be preserved; jumps remain possible.

questions.prompt: A program contains instructions at addresses 200, 201, 202, and 300. The program counter (PC) starts at 200. After each instruction, the PC is incremented by 1 unless there is a jump. The instruction at address 201 jumps to address 300 if its condition is satisfied; if the condition is not satisfied, the program continues at the next address. Which sequences give the addresses of the first three instructions executed, once when the condition is satisfied and once when it is not?
questions.explanation: Execution starts at 200 and proceeds normally to 201. If the condition is not satisfied there, address 202 follows. If it is satisfied, the PC jumps to 300. Thus, the two sequences are 200, 201, 202 and 200, 201, 300.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Both are encoded memory contents, but data and instructions have different agreed-upon interpretations: instructions follow the ISA encoding, while data follow their respective encoding.

questions.prompt: Which mapping correctly describes data and instructions?

options.text: Data are always ISA instructions; instructions are always decimal data.
Instructions reside only in the input/output unit, and data only in registers.
Assembly text is the only possible memory representation for instructions.
Data follow an agreed-upon binary interpretation; instructions are encoded according to the ISA and can be represented as assembly.

questions.explanation: The table distinguishes how data and instructions are interpreted, although both can reside in memory as encoded contents.

questions.prompt: A routine calls a second routine. Which approach correctly preserves the ability to return?

options.text: The return address is not saved because a nested call does not change it.
The stack frame is released before the nested call and is not set up again afterward.
The first return address is saved before the nested call and restored before returning.
All registers must always remain unchanged, regardless of the calling convention.

questions.explanation: A nested `jal` overwrites `ra`. The current return address must therefore be saved and restored before returning.

questions.prompt: At $PC=100$, `jal ra, 20` is executed. What values do `ra` and the new $PC$ have afterward?
questions.explanation: `jal` stores $PC+4=104$ in `ra` and sets $PC$ to $PC+20=120$. The other options confuse the return address with the jump target or calculate the offset incorrectly.

questions.prompt: Which combination correctly describes the stack and main memory?

options.text: The stack is in the input/output unit and is managed word by word without addresses.
The stack is in main memory, which is byte-addressed.
The stack is a memory with its own cells, independent of main memory.
The stack is located exclusively in registers and cannot be addressed.

questions.explanation: The stack is an area of byte-addressed main memory. It is not a technically separate memory.

questions.prompt: A program calls `printf` and is linked with a library. Which operations are part of linking? Select all correct statements; more than one answer may be correct.

options.text: The reference to `printf` is matched to an appropriate target.
Linking automatically changes Von Neumann into a Harvard architecture.
The call to `printf` is fully executed during linking.
The compiled program component and the required library are combined.
Address information is adjusted if necessary.

questions.explanation: Linking combines program components and libraries, resolves references such as the one to `printf`, and may adjust addresses. It does not execute the call or automatically change the memory architecture.

questions.prompt: A computer has shared main memory for programs and data, separate instruction and data caches, and a program area that cannot be modified. Which classification is correct?

options.text: A pure Von Neumann design with no separate memory handling
The hybrid form described; write protection is independent of it
Harvard architecture, because the program area cannot be modified
Self-modifying code, because programs reside in main memory

questions.explanation: Shared main memory with separate instruction and data caches is the hybrid form described. Write protection concerns how the area is handled and does not, by itself, answer the organizational question.

questions.prompt: A program starts at address $100$. The instruction at $101$ is a conditional jump to $200$; the condition is true. Which three addresses are executed first?
questions.explanation: Execution starts at $100$ and reaches the jump instruction at $101$. Because the condition is true, the target address $200$ follows instead of the sequential address $102$.

options.text: Programs reside outside main memory and are processed only by the input/output unit.

questions.prompt: Adjusting references during linking is the same as self-modifying code.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Linking combines compiled components and adjusts references or addresses. Self-modifying code, by contrast, changes its own program code.

questions.prompt: Which statements correctly connect the fundamental idea of the Von Neumann model with optimized program execution? Select all correct statements; more than one answer may be correct.

options.text: Conditional and unconditional jumps can depart from the sequential order.
A shared main memory automatically means a Harvard architecture.
Optimizations may change internal register allocation and instruction order as long as the observable behavior is preserved.
Self-modifying code is required for every jump.
The computer’s structure remains independent of the specific problem; the program controls the computer.

questions.explanation: Programs control the general-purpose computer model, optimizations may change the internal implementation, and jumps can depart from the sequence. Statements b and e contradict the concepts described.

questions.prompt: In general, instructions are executed sequentially; jumps determine when execution continues at a ___ location.

options.text: different
non-addressable
only higher
same

questions.explanation: A jump sets execution to continue at another location in the program. Without a jump, execution would continue in sequential order.

questions.prompt: In principle, how can the same memory contain both data and instructions?

options.text: Data and instructions must always reside in separate main memories.
Instructions are interpreted exclusively as decimal data and data exclusively as jumps.
Instructions do not reside in main memory, but only in the control unit.
Both are encoded memory contents; data are interpreted according to their agreed-upon encoding, and instructions according to the ISA.

questions.explanation: Both data and instructions reside in shared memory as encoded contents. Their use determines the appropriate interpretation: an agreed-upon data encoding or ISA encoding.

levels.title: In Practice: Computers in Everyday Life

questions.prompt: You open a navigation app, a music app, and Sudoku in sequence on the same smartphone. What is the architectural idea behind this?

options.text: Prologue and epilogue: each app thereby has its own processor.
The Von Neumann model: a general-purpose computer is controlled by different programs to perform different tasks.
Harvard architecture: a separate main memory is installed for each app.
Linking: the operating system reconnects the hardware each time it starts.

questions.explanation: The Von Neumann model separates the computer’s structure from the specific problem: the same device can perform very different tasks when controlled by different programs.

questions.prompt: You compile a C program in static-link mode that uses `printf`. When the executable is created, the reference to the library function is resolved. Which step is this?

options.text: Epilogue
Conditional jump
Linking
Division into Harvard memories

questions.explanation: During linking, compiled program components and libraries are combined and references such as the one to `printf` are resolved; in static-link mode, this happens when the executable is created.

questions.prompt: A memory chip labels an area as 1 KiB. How many Bytes is that?
questions.explanation: The prefix Ki denotes a power of two: 1 KiB = 2^10 Byte = 1024 Byte.

questions.prompt: When a function in an image-editing program is called, local variables and saved registers are set up. When the function returns, this space is released. What are these two boundary phases called?

options.text: Fetch and decode
Linking and loading
Harvard and Von Neumann
Prologue and epilogue

questions.explanation: The prologue sets up the stack frame and saves necessary values; the epilogue restores them and tears down the stack frame.

questions.prompt: A sensor provides an unsigned measurement with 12 bits. How many distinct bit patterns, or values, are possible?
questions.explanation: Each of the 12 bits can be 0 or 1, so there are 2^12 = 4096 distinct combinations.

questions.prompt: A processor uses the same main memory for instructions and data, but has separate instruction and data caches. Which description fits best?

options.text: Self-modifying code
Pure Harvard architecture with completely separate memories
A stack frame with two return addresses
Modified Harvard architecture: shared main memory with separate instruction and data caches

questions.explanation: This is a modified Harvard organization: programs and data share main memory, while the instruction and data caches are separate.

questions.prompt: You are documenting a truth table for five binary inputs. How many rows does it need to include every input combination?
questions.explanation: Each of the five binary inputs has two possibilities; that gives 2^5 = 32 combinations and therefore 32 rows.

questions.prompt: An operating system marks the program area as write-protected. This automatically means the architecture is Harvard. Is that correct?

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Write protection governs whether a memory area may be modified. Harvard, by contrast, describes the separation of program and data memory—these are two different questions.

questions.prompt: A game checks `if (Leben == 0)` and then jumps to “Game Over”; otherwise, the next game step runs. What allows execution to depart from the normal instruction order?

options.text: Separate data memory
A conditional jump
The prologue of a stack frame
Linking a library

questions.explanation: Conditional jumps change the normal sequential flow and continue at another location depending on the result.
